examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Complement of a Span
examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors that span the subspace $H$ as $\mathbf{h}_1$ and $\mathbf{h}_2.$ 

A vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065672/assets/ed0e0a3a78ff25be588f62627ffd5bae4074f6c59b8e88ad160e4407253ae6dd.png) belongs to $H^{\perp}$ if $\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{h}_1=0$ and $\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{h}_2=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065672/assets/af507041d4aa3cc7dfb415afc672b5a7875f9f1a27acced81505797e5f92d7e0.png) 

We write the corresponding augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{3}{2} & \frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, we have $2$ pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd ones), so $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation we get $x_2=-\dfrac{1}{3}x_3.$ Substituting this into first equation, we obtain $x_1 = -\dfrac{1}{3}x_3.$

So, the general solution to the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065672/assets/34b29c1902a7c441b2ac15be91ffb60b8856ab7dc2706146d09eb02f081827ba.png)

Therefore, our orthogonal complement is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065672/assets/496154a4d67c0b7861da038306f1d5cc65188cc036cf8514b24603c7ce4cd948.png)

feedback.problem:
Consider the vector subspace $H=\text{Span}{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 0 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ -11\end{aligned}]}.$ Which of the following vectors belong to ${H}^{⊥}?$

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -14 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 14 \\ 6\end{aligned}]
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors that span the subspace $H$ as ${h}_{1}$ and ${h}_{2}.$ 

Now, a vector $v$ belongs to ${H}^{⊥}$ if $v$ is orthogonal to the set of vectors that spans the subspace $H.$ So, we have to find the products ${v}_{i}\cdot {h}_{j}$ for $i=1,2,3$ and  $j=1,2.$  

- For ${v}_{1}$, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {h}_{1} & =5\cdot (-6)+(-2)\cdot 0+6\cdot 5=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {h}_{2} & =5\cdot 2+(-2)\cdot 4+6\cdot (-11)=-64\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, ${v}_{1}\notin {H}^{⊥}.$

- For ${v}_{2}$, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\cdot {h}_{1} & =5\cdot (-6)+(-14)\cdot 0+(-6)\cdot 5=-60\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, ${v}_{2}\notin {H}^{⊥}.$ We do not need to test ${v}_{2}\cdot {h}_{2}.$

- For ${v}_{3}$, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3}\cdot {h}_{1} & =5\cdot (-6)+14\cdot 0+6\cdot 5=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{3}\cdot {h}_{2} & =5\cdot 2+14\cdot 4+6\cdot (-11)=0 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${v}_{3}\in {H}^{⊥}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "${v}_{3}$ only".
